strengths: Addresses a practical and timely problem: generating graphics-ready 3D scenes with PBR materials rather than appearance-only generation

Introduces PanoX, a valuable synthetic panoramic dataset with comprehensive multimodal annotations (geometry + materials) covering both indoor and outdoor scenes, addressing a documented data scarcity
Comprehensive quantitative evaluation at component level with substantial improvements over baselines (e.g., albedo PSNR 17.755 vs 10.906 for best baseline)
Thorough ablation analysis of cross-modal adapter architectures (Table 4) with clear justification for design choices, including both in-domain and out-of-domain evaluation
End-to-end demonstration of practical pipeline from single image to graphics-compatible 3D scenes with PBR, relighting, and physical simulation in Blender
Clear presentation with well-designed figures and comprehensive experimental results across perception tasks (intrinsic decomposition, geometry estimation, generation, completion)
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: core contribution is straightforward application of LoRA adapters on pre-trained flow matching models; the unified formulation (Eq. 3) is a direct extension without significant conceptual innovation; adapter design choices are conventional

Core claim of 'graphics-ready' 3D scenes is undermined by acknowledged quality issues: metallic prediction performs poorly in generalization, distance estimation produces 'bumpy reconstructed 3D surfaces', and authors state pre-trained 2D priors have limited benefits for PBR material estimation

Critical gap: no quantitative metrics for final 3D scene quality; missing perceptual user studies; no comparison of full pipeline output with other panoramic generation methods (LayerPano3D, DreamCube, SceneDreamer360); Figure 8 shows only visual examples without validation

Dataset contribution overstated: only 8 large-scale scenes (5 indoor, 3 outdoor) despite 'large-scale' framing; 60K panoramic images from just 6 training scenes limits diversity; out-of-domain evaluation uses only 2 scenes; heavy reliance on Structured3D and HDR360-UHD for training

Seam continuity workaround required: acknowledged difficulty learning ERP panorama continuity necessitates horizontal blending from prior work (LayerPano3D), suggesting fundamental architectural limitations for panoramic data

Computational efficiency not addressed: no inference time, training time, or memory requirements; batch size of 1 during training indicates memory constraints; acknowledged 'slow inference efficiency' is not quantified

Incomplete experimental comparisons: MoGe trains on 21 large-scale datasets vs OmniX's smaller setup (unfair comparison despite authors' acknowledgment); limited baselines for panoramic-specific tasks; missing comparisons with other panoramic 3D generation methods

Counterintuitive ablation results without sufficient investigation: joint material/geometry modeling underperforms independent modeling (Tables 6-7) contrary to expectations, but explanations are speculative rather than mechanistic
Reproducibility concerns: no code or dataset release mentioned; proprietary UE5 dependency; missing implementation details; no public benchmark proposed for community evaluation
Statistical rigor absent: no error bars, confidence intervals, or significance testing; single test sets per split; out-of-domain evaluation on only 2 scenes is too limited

strengths: Well-motivated practical problem: Addresses the genuine gap between panoramic appearance generation and graphics-ready intrinsic properties (geometry, materials)
Comprehensive unified framework: Clean generalization (Eqs. 1-3) elegantly unifies generation, perception, and completion tasks across modalities
Effective adapter architecture: Separate-Adapter design is well-validated through systematic ablations (Table 4), achieving best perception performance

Strong empirical results on core perception tasks: Achieves state-of-the-art material estimation (albedo PSNR 17.76 vs 10.91, metallic 18.87 vs 14.45) and best normal prediction (27.14° vs 97.19°) with less training data than competitors
Valuable dataset contribution: PanoX is the first panoramic dataset with both dense geometry and PBR material annotations across indoor/outdoor scenes, addressing documented community gap
End-to-end demonstrable pipeline: Complete pathway from single image to graphics-compatible 3D scenes with relighting and physics simulation, showing practical utility
Thorough experimental validation: Comprehensive comparisons, detailed ablations (Tables 4-7), in-the-wild generalization results, and supplementary analysis
Excellent presentation: Clear writing, well-structured narrative, informative visualizations, and accessible methodology
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty in core components: Primarily applies off-the-shelf FLUX.1-dev with standard LoRA adapters; Separate-Adapter is a straightforward design choice without theoretical justification

Acknowledged critical limitations undermine applicability: Euclidean distance prediction produces 'bumpy surfaces' with 49% gap to SOTA (AbsRel 0.158 vs MoGe 0.106); metallic prediction 'performs poorly in generalization'; both are essential for graphics pipelines

Seam continuity workaround suggests fundamental model-data mismatch: DiT struggles with ERP panorama topology; addressed via borrowed horizontal blending from LayerPano3D rather than principled solution

Dataset scale and diversity limitations: Only 8 scenes (10k instances) entirely synthetic; out-of-domain evaluation uses merely 2 held-out scenes; limited scene type diversity (stores, warehouses, wilderness)

Insufficient 3D reconstruction evaluation: Metrics are predominantly 2D (PSNR, LPIPS, angular error); no quantitative 3D geometry quality metrics; applications section (4.5) provides only qualitative results with no relighting/simulation accuracy metrics
Comparison fairness concerns: Many baselines not designed for panoramas; workarounds required (e.g., multi-frame rendering for DiffusionRenderer); several methods have missing panoramic results
Generalization and reproducibility issues: Training on inaccessible Ascend 910B NPUs; no code/dataset release mentioned; limited in-the-wild evaluation mostly in appendix; no inference time analysis

Joint modeling ablation raises concerns: Joint geometry modeling (distance + normal) hurts rather than helps performance (Table 7); explained as data scarcity but fundamental limitation unresolved, suggesting method is data-hungry

strengths: Comprehensive unified framework effectively extending 2D flow matching to panoramic generation, perception, and completion with solid engineering
Strong experimental validation across multiple tasks with thorough ablations demonstrating the value of proposed components (circular sync, modality adapters)
Circular synchronization is a principled solution to panoramic seams, achieving cleaner boundaries than prior latent-level blending methods without fine-tuning
PanoX dataset addresses genuine gap as first panorama dataset with dense geometry and material annotations covering both indoor/outdoor scenes
Honest and comprehensive limitations discussion acknowledging distance prediction errors, metallic generalization issues, and fundamental incompatibility of 2D priors with PBR estimation
Clear presentation with informative figures, well-organized supplementary material, and good ablation studies
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty of core components: circular synchronization is intuitive but straightforward (circular padding + attention masking); modality-specific adapters are essentially separate LoRAs; unified formulation is direct generalization of flow matching

Significant gap between claims and acknowledged limitations: paper claims 'graphics-ready 3D scenes suitable for PBR' but admits distance prediction causes 'bumpy reconstructed 3D surfaces' and that '2D priors have limited benefits for PBR material estimation'—undermining core contribution

Dataset limitations: synthetic-only (Unreal Engine 5) with only 8 environments (6 for training), lacking real-world diversity; domain gap to wild panoramas not thoroughly studied; scale modest compared to some scene datasets

Unequal comparisons complicate claims: MoGe trains on 9.0M depth annotations vs. 0.087M for OmniX; CubeDiff improvements are incremental (FID +2.1 on Laval, KID higher); panorama-specific adaptation of baselines sometimes unfair

Insufficient material estimation analysis: metallic prediction shows poor generalization (acknowledged), roughness PSNR ~16–18 is modest; no quantitative evaluation of rendering accuracy or analysis of root causes

Experimental design gaps: no error bars or statistical significance; batch size 1 per GPU lacks justification; no human perceptual evaluation; resolution fixed at 512×1024 without comparison impact analysis

Incomplete ablations: no isolated assessment of circular synchronization contribution; limited analysis of why Separate-Adapter works beyond numerical results; joint distance-normal modeling shows no benefit but not deeply analyzed

Generalization concerns: strong out-of-domain results on synthetic PanoX still synthetic; wild panorama results (Fig. S3) relegated to supplementary with minimal analysis; metallic generalization failure on real images not addressed

strengths: Comprehensive unified framework addressing panorama generation, perception, and completion in a principled manner, demonstrating strong empirical results across all tasks

Well-motivated circular synchronization approach that correctly identifies and solves seam discontinuity as a fundamental structural issue in spatial operators, shown to outperform post-hoc approaches (Figure 10)
Thorough ablation studies validating design choices, including adapter architectures (Table 5) and component effectiveness, with clear empirical evidence for each decision
Strong experimental results achieving state-of-the-art on panorama generation (FID 7.4 on Laval Indoor) and intrinsic decomposition tasks across multiple metrics
PanoX dataset addresses a genuine research gap with dense multimodal annotations across indoor/outdoor scenes, and clear positioning relative to existing datasets
Effective demonstration of practical end-to-end applicability through PBR-ready 3D scene generation with multiple applications (exploration, relighting, simulation)
Clear presentation with comprehensive related work, transparent methodology, and honest limitations discussion
weaknesses: Distance and metallic material prediction remain significantly inaccurate (acknowledged as producing 'bumpy surfaces' and 'poor generalization'), directly undermining the core claim of graphics-ready 3D scenes and limiting practical PBR utility

Individual technical components are incremental: circular padding is straightforward, LoRA adapters are established techniques, and unified formulation is a direct extension of prior equations without significant conceptual novelty
PanoX dataset has limited scale and diversity (only 8 synthetic environments, 10K instances) compared to contemporary datasets, and synthetic-only nature limits real-world applicability claims

Heavy reliance on synthetic data for evaluation; real-world validation relegated to supplementary material; no quantitative evaluation of final 3D scene generation quality or user studies validating perceived quality

Joint geometry modeling (distance-normal) provides no benefit (Table S4), suggesting the framework fails to capture relationships between correlated concepts, raising concerns about geometric understanding
Unfair comparisons in some cases: MoGe comparison uses 100x more training data (9.0M vs 0.087M annotations); some baselines designed for different modalities
Minimal benefit from spatial conditioning (camera rays improve normal estimation by only 0.66°), questioning whether the model effectively captures spatial relationships
Reproducibility concerns: no code availability mentioned, project page URL not provided, some experimental details vague; limited discussion of computational costs relative to baselines
